title: The one where Joe gets to combine his nerdy interests: theatre and la...
transcript: Why did the Wicked movie change this lyric in No Good Deed? I saw someone asking this and I think I have an answer. If you didn't catch it, it's a very small change. So on the original cast recording she sings “since I cannot succeed, Fiyero, saving you” versus in the movie “and since I can't succeed, Fiyero, saving you.” I caught this in the theater and it did trip me up for a second, but then when I thought about it, I realized this lyric actually is a lot better, and it has to do with the way the music and the grammar of the sentences are working together (Or not) Because this lyric, I think, was desperately in need of a conjunction. Especially with the musical phrasing, It kinda sounds like she's saying “I'm wicked through and through, since I cannot succeed, Fiyero, saving you.” As in “that's the reason I'm wicked through and through” And sure you can keep listening and be like “oh wait, no, that was the beginning of the next sentence, not the end of the last sentence.” You can figure it out, but at that point it's too late. The lyric was already more confusing than it should’ve been. Because it's written to be performed live, the best musical theatre lyric writing is designed to strike the audience's ear as correctly as possible, on the first listen. This little change completely clears up that grammatical ambiguity by making a clear distinction between clauses; “I'm wicked through and through *and* since I can't succeed, Fiyero, saving you…. I promise, no good deed will I attempt to do again.” But naturally with the word “and” stuck in there, you've added a syllable, so in order to keep it scanning correctly with the music, you have to remove a syllable, hence changing “cannot” to “can't”
